summary: The note describes the linguistic diversity of Namibia, which has a small population but languages from several families, including Indo-European, Bantu, and Khoisan. It explains the shift in official language status from the South African administration period, when Afrikaans, German, and English were equal official languages, to independence in 1990, when English became the sole official language. It also notes why German and Afrikaans were stigmatised and how English spread through the anti-apartheid movement.
one_line: Overview of Namibia's diverse language families and the change from multiple official languages to English as sole official language after 1990 independence.
key_facts: Namibia has a scant population but is home to a wide diversity of languages.
Namibian languages come from multiple families: Indo-European, Bantu, and the various Khoisan families.
When Namibia was administered by South Africa, Afrikaans, German, and English enjoyed an equal status as official languages.
Upon Namibian independence in 1990, English was enshrined as the nation's sole official language in the constitution of Namibia.
German and Afrikaans were stigmatised as having colonial overtones after independence.
Mandela's Youth League and the 1951 Defiance Campaign spread English among the masses as the language of the campaign against apartheid.
English spread among the masses through the campaign against apartheid led by Mandela's Youth League and the 1951 Defiance Campaign.
